docs.description: Case name: Board of Ed. of Kiryas Joel Village School Dist. v. Grumet Opinion filed: 1994-06-27 Docket No.: 93-517 Citations: • 129 L. Ed. 2d 546 • 114 S. Ct. 2481 • 512 U.S. 687 • 1994 U.S. LEXIS 4830 Case holding summaries: • “[O]ur [Establishment Clause] analysis does not end with the text of the statute at issue.” • "[A] principle at the heart of the Establishment Clause [is] that government should not prefer one religion to another, or religion to irreligion." • "the statute before us fails the test of neutrality." • " 'A proper respect for both the Free Exercise and the Establishment Clauses compels the State to pursue a course of "neutrality" toward religion.' " (quoting Committee for Pub. Educ. & Religious Liberty v. Nyquist, 413 U.S. 756, 792-93, 93 S.Ct. 2955, 37 L.Ed.2d 948 (1973 • " 'A proper respect for both the Free Exercise and the Establishment Clauses compels the State to pursue a course of "neutrality" toward religion.' " (quoting Committee for Pub. Educ. & Religious Liberty v. Nyquist, 413 U.S. 756, 792-93, 93 S.Ct. 2955, 37 L.Ed.2d 948 (1973)) • Establishment Clause prevents delegating governmental power to religious group • upholding law exempting religious employers from Title VII • exemption of religious organizations from Title VII's prohibition of religious discrimination • accepting claim that peyote exemption for Native American Church requires peyote exemption for other religions that use that substance in their sacraments • reaching this result on statutory interpretation grounds • sign-language translator for deaf student • rejecting claim that peyote exemption requires marijuana exemption for Ethiopian Zion Coptic Church • "Faced with the choice between invalidation and extension of any controlledsubstances religious exemption, which would the political branches choose? It would take a court bolder than this one to predict . . . that extension, not invalidation, would be the probable choice" • finding a lack of any "`effective means of guaranteeing' " that governmental power will be neutrally employed under Lemon `s "`principal' or `primary effect' " prong • finding "`a fusion of governmental and religious functions' " under Lemon `s "entanglement" prong • uniting two strands of Free Speech Clause doctrine • military draft exemption for religious objectors • facially race-neutral laws can be invalidated on the basis of their effects only if "unexplainable on grounds other than race" • government may allow religious organizations to favor their own adherents in hiring, even for secular employment • New York City program permitting public school children to leave school for one hour a week for religious observance and instruction • government may allow public schools to release students during the schoolday to receive off-site religious education • military draft exemption for religious objectors • approving a program permitting early release of public school students to attend religious instruction • curing gender discrimination in the Aid to Families with Dependent Children program by extending benefits to children of unemployed mothers instead of denying benefits to children of unemployed fathers • upholding school bus service provided all pupils • looking at some aspects of religious law to determine the structure of the church, but refusing to look further into religious law to resolve the ultimate dispute • which also did not apply Lemon • exemption from drug laws for sacramental peyote use • legislatures may grant accommodations even when courts may not • "The limits of permissible state accommodation to religion are by no means co-extensive with the noninterference mandated by the Free Exercise Clause" • Establishment Clause prevents State from "participat[ing] in the affairs of any religious organizations or groups and vice versa " • government need not "be oblivious to impositions that legitimate exercises of state power may place on religious belief and practice" • general availability of benefits provided to religious groups necessary for compliance with Establishment Clause • “‘A proper respect for both the Free Exercise and the Establishment Clauses compels the State to pursue a course of ‘neutrality’ toward religion.’” (quoting Committee for Pub. Educ. & Religious Liberty v. Nyquist, 413 U.S. 756, 792-93 (1973)) • “[O]ur [Establishment Clause] analysis does not end with the text of the statute at issue.” • stating that the Religion Clauses "command[ ] neutrality" • emphasizing neutrality among religious sects is central to Establish Clause jurisprudence • " 'A proper respect for both the Free Exercise and the Establishment Clauses compels the State to pursue a course of neutrality toward religion,' favoring neither one religion over others nor religious adherents collectively over nonadherents." • "Our cases leave no doubt that in commanding neutrality the Religion Clauses do not require the government to be oblivious to impositions that legitimate exercises of state power may place on religious belief and practice." • “[U]nlike an administrative agency’s denial of an exemption 10 from a generally applicable law, which would be entitled to a judicial audience, a legislature’s 11 failure to enact a special law is itself unreviewable.” (internal citations and quotation marks 12 omitted) • "It is clear that neutrality as among religions must be honored." • “[A] principle at the heart of the Establishment 483 U.S. 327, 335 (1987 • "[A] principle at the heart of the Establishment Clause [is] that government should not prefer one religion to another, or religion to irreligion." • stating that "a principle at the heart of the Establishment Clause [is] that government should not prefer one religion to another, or religion to irreligion." • assuming the existence of standing in a suit brought by New York State taxpayers challenging state statute • invalidating statute creating school district coextensive with religious community that had valid purpose of providing special education services, but was unnecessarily tailored to promote sectarian aims • explaining that this principle is "at the heart of the Establishment Clause" • recognizing the role of courts in “safeguarding a principle at the heart of the Establish­ ment Clause, that government should not prefer one reli­ gion to another, or religion to irreligion” • invalidating a state law that created a new school district for a single religious community • drawing a separate school district for one religion violates the Establishment Clause
